items.stem: The first-person point of view most significantly affects the reader's understanding of the narrator's final decision to record the compass as "missing" by:
choices: showing that the narrator's account includes facts but is shaped by a desire to protect a preferred version of his memory
establishing that the aunt deliberately concealed the compass in order to test whether the narrator could be trusted
presenting the inventory as an objective record that overrides the narrator's uncertainty about what happened
revealing the uncle's private intention in lending the compass while leaving the narrator's actions fully certain
items.stimulus: By the time I returned to Wren Island, my aunt had painted the porch steps the same blue as the sea, though she insisted the color had been chosen before I was born. I had come to inventory my late uncle's workshop, and each evening she asked whether I had found the brass compass. She asked lightly, but I heard accusation in the question, as if the missing object were evidence of a promise I had broken. The workshop's drawers held receipts, bird bones, and a nest of rusted keys, but no compass. On the third day, I found it in my own suitcase, wrapped in a wool sock; I could not recall packing it. My aunt saw it and laughed, saying that my uncle had lent it to me on my last visit; her version was supported by a salt-stained note in his handwriting, but I read the note as a practical joke because that interpretation left my memory undisturbed. When the ferry horn sounded, she said she had expected me to remember, and I realized that my inventory had been less about objects than about proving I had been trusted. I left the compass on the table, yet wrote in the inventory that it was "missing."
items.explanation: The narrator admits that he read the note as a practical joke "because that interpretation left my memory undisturbed," then records the compass as "missing" even after finding it. Because the events are filtered through his first-person perspective, the factual discovery and his self-protective interpretation appear together, making the final record psychologically revealing but not fully objective.

Curator Mr. Vale had left a note asking me to polish the glass around the museum's newest painting, a stormy harbor scene. From my station, I watched him pause before the painting whenever visitors approached, then step behind a column until they moved on. I decided he was avoiding questions about why the painting had no artist's signature. When I finally asked him about it, he smiled and said he was listening to the visitors describe what they thought the missing name should be. Only then did I notice that he carried a small notebook, filling it with their guesses. The painting, he explained, had been made by his sister, who had refused to sign it after losing her sight. I had spent the morning inventing a private drama for Mr. Vale, while he had been quietly collecting other people's words.

items.stem: Taken together, the narrator's initial description of Eli and the concluding admission primarily establish that the narrator's account is shaped by which feature of point of view?
choices: It presents the narrator's access to Eli as indirect, allowing later evidence to revise the first interpretation without settling Eli's motives.

items.stimulus: I had always thought my brother Eli's silence during town meetings was shyness, because from my seat beside him I saw only his lowered eyes and his thumb worrying a paper cup. Years later, while sorting our late mother's notebooks, I found Eli's penciled maps of sewer grates, each marked with dates and arrows toward the river. The maps made his silence look less like withdrawal than attention, though I could not tell whether he had been documenting a danger or merely the routes he walked to avoid crowds. When I asked him about them, he laughed and said, "You make a mystery of ordinary errands"; then he folded the map along lines that erased the river. I wanted his joke to settle the matter, but at the next meeting I noticed him watching the mayor's new drainage plan with the same fixed concentration. From where I sat, the plan's blue lines resembled his old arrows, a resemblance I knew might belong more to my need for a pattern than to his intentions. Eli later told a reporter that he had never opposed the plan, yet he slipped me a note saying he hoped I would keep the notebooks "until people ask the right question." I still cannot say whether Eli was warning the town, teasing me, or preserving a private geography; I can say only that my first explanation of him was the one least tested.

Uncle Ren greeted me with a nod and placed a stopped pocket watch in my palm. Because I had never opened one, I watched his hands instead of trying to copy them.

When the first customer arrived, Uncle Ren listened while she described the watch's failure. He laid the watch beside three tiny screwdrivers and tightened his jaw. By noon, the watch ticked again, although its second hand moved unevenly. I had not asked Uncle Ren what had troubled him because he was already studying the mechanism again. items.stem: How does the narrator's limited perspective shape the reader's understanding of the uncle in the first two paragraphs?
choices: It establishes that the uncle dislikes both the mayor and the town's traditions, even though he continues the repair.
It reveals that the narrator understands the uncle's feelings better than the mayor does because the narrator works beside him.

items.stimulus:
On the morning the town rehung its weather vane, I carried my uncle's toolbox across the square, expecting the job to be as dull as he had promised. The town had hired him to repair the copper swallow that pointed toward the river, though I suspected he had accepted only because he disliked refusing anyone who asked in person. I expected him to complain about the mayor's deadlines and the courthouse roof. Instead, he polished each feather with the care he usually reserved for objects that belonged to our family.

Mayor Venn arrived before we had finished, declaring that the swallow had watched over the town for nearly a century. I had heard that story before, but only from people standing below the roof, where the bird looked less like a guardian than a small stain against the sky. When the mayor asked whether the vane would be ready for the Founders' Day parade, my uncle gave a noncommittal shrug. I took his silence as another sign that the project meant little to him.

After the mayor left, my uncle told me that his mother had painted the first design for the vane, using a swallow because she believed returning birds made promises visible. He had kept the detail quiet because he did not want the town to treat his work as a sentimental favor. I realized then that I had mistaken his silence for indifference, just as I had mistaken the weathered bird for something ordinary. By noon, I still disliked the mayor's grand speeches, but I understood why my uncle had polished every feather before anyone could see them.

From my upstairs office, I could hear visitors below but could not see their faces unless I leaned over the stairwell. On the fourth morning, a boy asked why the station map showed no route beyond the inlet, and Mara answered that the route had vanished after the 1968 storm. She did not say whether the boats had vanished, the map had vanished, or merely the town’s willingness to remember them. I assumed she was correcting a child, not the institution that had hired me.

That afternoon, while checking a drawer the museum had marked empty, I found the first director’s notebook. One entry called the bell “a signal for boats”; another called it “a ritual for those waiting,” and a final instruction told staff to omit both descriptions because “the station’s purpose should be clear.” I wanted these contradictions to settle whether Mara remembered accurately; instead, they showed me that the archive had been shaped by someone else’s wish for clarity. When Mara asked whether the bell belonged in the exhibit, I answered yes, but added, “with the uncertainty intact.” I still could not say what the bell had meant on any particular morning; I could say why the label “unverified” had been too easy.

items.stimulus:
When I was asked to write wall text for Mara Venn’s 1934 mural River of Hands, I expected to summarize its commission, not defend its silences. City records call the mural a celebration of cooperative labor, and a newspaper article from the same year praises its civic pride. Yet my grandmother, who cleaned offices beneath the mural, remembered that workers posed for Venn only after their shifts and said the painted hands looked “too clean.” Her remark initially seemed anecdotal, but it led me to inspect a payroll ledger in which women and migrants appear as names but not as contributors to the dedication.

I therefore resisted calling the mural either propaganda or hidden protest. Venn’s letters, which I read in an archive, praise the city’s investment and complain that officials wanted “a picture people can stand beneath without arguing.” That sentence does not prove she opposed the officials; perhaps she wanted accessibility, or perhaps she knew that any argument would be edited out. Still, in the mural’s upper corner, a small unpainted rectangle interrupts the orderly hands; the restoration report labels it damage, but Venn’s sketch leaves it blank.

Because I had heard my grandmother’s story, I was tempted to treat the rectangle as a deliberate accusation; because the records could not establish that, I described it as a space whose meaning remains contested. The final label says the mural “joins civic optimism to the evidence of labor’s exclusions,” wording that sounds less certain than either the celebratory plaque or my grandmother’s verdict. Some visitors may find this caution evasive, but it records the difference between what I can document and what I have inherited. I used to think responsible interpretation meant choosing between official history and family memory; now I see my task as showing how each illuminates the other while neither possesses the whole wall.

items.stem: The passage is primarily shaped by the narrator's perspective as someone who:
choices: Uses a changing interpretation of the map to examine the assumptions that later viewers bring to historical artifacts.
Describes a classroom discovery mainly to show students that visual symbols are more reliable than written records.
Attempts to reconstruct Elias Venn's private intentions from every available physical detail of the map.
Rejects the town council's political influence in order to defend the map as an accurate portrait of the valley.
items.stimulus:
At the municipal archive, I began studying a 1648 map of the river valley expecting its omissions to reveal the mapmaker's ignorance. Instead, the broad uninked margins seemed deliberate: they left room for the roads and farms that the town council, which commissioned the map, wished to claim as orderly. I could not ask the mapmaker, Elias Venn, whether he intended that effect; the surviving ledger records his payment but not his purpose. Still, the map's confident borders made me suspect that uncertainty belonged less to Venn than to me, a later reader trained to treat maps as neutral records.

When I first described the drawing to my students, I called the tiny figures along the river decorative. Looking again, I noticed that each figure faced the town rather than the water, and I revised my account: the figures may have marked who was entitled to approach the river. That revision did not recover Venn's private intention, but it exposed the assumptions my first description had smuggled in. I had been asking what the figures represented, a question that made the map answer in the language of objects; the more revealing question was whom the map allowed to appear as an observer.

The council's map, then, is not simply a portrait of a landscape but a performance of authority, although calling it propaganda would claim more certainty than the evidence permits.
